First, I provided some examples of command hallucinations from the book "The Silent Boy" by Andrew Taylor. Command hallucinations are voices that instruct a person to do something, which can range from simple commands to threats.

Next, I discussed olfactory phantosmia and parosmia, which are distortions to the sense of smell. Phantosmia is the perception of an odor that is not present, while parosmia is the perception of a different scent than the actual odor. These conditions can result from various causes, including infections, nasal polyps, dental problems, migraines, head injuries, seizures, strokes, or brain tumors. Environmental exposures, such as smoking or chemical exposure, can also cause these distortions.

Lastly, I shared some statistics on the decline in leisure reading among young people. According to a study, the percentage of high school seniors who never or rarely read for pleasure has increased from 17% in the 1970s to 27% in the mid-2010s. Additionally, twelfth-graders read an average of two fewer books per year in the mid-2010s than in the mid-1970s, and a third did not read books at all. These trends were consistent across sexual, racial, and socioeconomic lines.

The Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at Oxford University found that 45% of people aged 18 to 24 in the U.S. and U.K. cited social media as their first source of news.
